THE TIDE CLOCK
An original story for multipage comic testing.

At four in the morning, the harbor clock rang thirteen times. Nia counted each note from the lighthouse kitchen, her hands wrapped around a cup of tea that had gone cold. The clock had no thirteenth bell. She knew because she had polished its twelve brass hammers with her grandfather every autumn until he could no longer climb the tower stairs. Outside, the tide lay unusually still. Fishing boats rested against their ropes without knocking the wooden quay. Even the gulls were silent. When the final note faded, a thin blue line appeared beneath the kitchen door. Nia opened it and found a brass bird standing on the step. One wing was folded neatly; the other trailed a wire as fine as hair. In its beak it held a scrap of sailcloth embroidered with the old harbor map. A circle marked the station that everyone said the sea had swallowed.

Nia put the bird on the kitchen table. It tapped three times beside the map and opened a small glass door in its chest. Inside, a wheel turned backward. Her grandfather had made mechanical toys, but never anything this patient or this precise. Nia fetched his repair notebook from the cupboard beneath the stairs. Between diagrams of lamp gears she found the same bird drawn in green pencil. Under it were six words: When the clock forgets, follow water. The handwriting looked hurried. On the next page he had sketched the harbor before the sea wall existed, with a narrow channel running under the present market square. Nia traced the channel with a finger. Someone had recently added a red cross at its mouth. She checked the windows and the empty path outside. Then she packed the notebook, wrapped the bird in a clean towel, and went to find Arun at the ferry workshop.

Arun was trying to persuade an old engine to start when Nia arrived. He listened to the thirteen bells story without interrupting, which worried her more than disbelief would have. Finally he pulled a wet copper token from his pocket. The same blue light glowed around its edge. He had found it inside a ferry pump the previous evening, although the intake filter should have stopped anything that large. They laid token and bird together. The wheel in the bird's chest stopped turning backward. It pointed its beak toward the market. Arun reached for his tool bag and the workshop tide chart. Every prediction for the coming week had been scratched out. In their place, his apprentice had written that the water gauges were disagreeing. One showed low tide, another high, and the third had cracked. Arun left a note on the engine and joined Nia in the pale street. Behind them, a ferry horn sounded a long uncertain question.

The market vendors were setting up beneath yellow awnings. Baskets of oranges sat beside coils of rope and jars of pickled lemons. Nothing looked like a drowned station. Nia asked Mira, who sold secondhand books, whether there had ever been a channel under the square. Mira closed her ledger and studied the sailcloth. She remembered her mother speaking about a water gate, built before the harbor wall. The gate had carried floodwater around the town instead of through it. When the railway arrived, the channel was covered, and its maintenance keys went missing. Mira thought the station's waiting room had become part of a cellar. She led them behind a stack of empty crates to a staircase nobody used. Damp air rose from below. The brass bird wriggled free of its towel and hopped down the first step. Nia followed, one hand on the wall, while Arun held a lamp above the dark opening.

At the bottom they found a ticket window, a broken bench, and a timetable printed with destinations that no longer existed. Water covered the floor to the depth of a fingernail. The bird crossed it without making ripples. Behind the ticket counter stood a broad iron door with three circular sockets. Arun tried the copper token in the smallest. It fit, but the other two remained empty. Nia opened the notebook again. A drawing showed a lamp, a bridge, and a garden, each connected to one of the sockets. Beneath them was a warning: Do not force the gate while the reservoirs disagree. A distant rumble moved through the stones. Water crept across the timetable glass. Mira marked its height with a pencil. They had less time than they thought. On the reverse of the sailcloth, newly visible in the damp, someone had stitched a sentence: The town must remember together.

They returned to daylight and separated only far enough to ask questions. Mira stayed at the market to find anyone who remembered the old waterworks. Arun went to the footbridge, where maintenance crews stored retired machinery. Nia returned to the lighthouse because the lamp symbol matched a gear in her grandfather's drawings. As she climbed the spiral stairs, she noticed salt crystals forming on the inside of the windows. The sea was pressing upward through hidden spaces. In the lantern room, the brass bird pecked at a loose panel below the lens. Behind it lay a second token, silver instead of copper, tied to a length of blue ribbon. Nia recognized the ribbon from her grandmother's summer hat. She sat on the top stair for a moment, surprised by the tenderness of the discovery. This was not a message from strangers. Her family had left a job unfinished, and trusted someone else to finish it.

A letter folded around the silver token explained only part of the mystery. Years before, the old water gate had begun to stick. The council planned a new pumping station, so the keepers had shut the gate and distributed its three keys among people who understood the harbor. The new station was never completed. Records disappeared during an office move, and the closed channel slowly filled with silt. Her grandfather had built the bird as a warning device linked to the oldest tide gauge. He had hoped never to hear it ring the clock's extra note. Nia read the letter twice. At the bottom, in a different hand, her grandmother had added that a warning was useful only if people could understand what to do next. Nia took the lighthouse signal flags from their drawer. She would need help explaining this to a town that was already waking to flooded doorsteps.

Arun found the bridge token inside a hollow railing cap. Getting it out required a borrowed wrench, two cups of patience, and the assistance of a child named Dev, whose small fingers could reach where adult hands could not. Dev insisted on coming back to the market with them. He had seen water running uphill beside his school, and wanted an answer before his teacher asked for one. At the market, Mira had gathered six elderly residents around a chalk map. Their recollections disagreed about names and dates but agreed about the garden. Before it became a public orchard, it had been a settling reservoir. Its lowest wall contained a spillway feeding the channel. The third key was no longer needed; the bridge token had opened a compartment containing it. The real problem was elsewhere. Someone had built a storage shed across the spillway, and behind it the orchard was filling like a bowl.

The town coordinator arrived wearing boots over her office clothes. She listened to the residents, looked at the map, and asked for evidence they could check quickly. Nia showed the letter and the bird. Arun brought readings from three pumps. Mira produced an old property survey with the channel clearly marked. Together, these were enough. The coordinator sent crews to move goods from the orchard shed, but she would not let anyone open an unknown gate beneath an occupied square. They needed to understand where the released water would go. Nia felt irritation rise, then recognized the fairness of the question. Her grandfather's warning had said the same thing in fewer words. Dev pointed to a faded line on the survey. It ran beyond the lighthouse to a rocky inlet used only by seals. If the outlet still existed, they could inspect it before making a decision. Nia and Arun took a small boat along the outer wall.

The inlet looked peaceful until they noticed bubbles rising in a straight line beside the rocks. Beneath the surface, a buried pipe was trying to breathe. Arun lowered a sounding pole while Nia held the boat steady. The pole struck an iron grille covered in weed and driftwood. A large log lay diagonally across it, pinned by years of smaller debris. Opening the gate while the grille was blocked would send pressure back toward the market. They tied a bright float over the obstruction and returned to the quay. By then, volunteers were carrying library boxes upstairs. A woman had parked her bicycle sideways to keep children away from a flooded alley. Nobody needed a heroic speech. They needed clear instructions and tools. Arun asked for the harbor winch. Nia asked for enough people to pull safely from shore. Dev fetched the coordinator, who approved the work after checking the ropes and the tide.

The first pull failed. The log shifted a finger's width, then settled into the mud again. Arun stopped everyone before a rope could fray. He sketched the angle of the grille on a piece of packing board and moved the shore pulley farther inland. Mira organized two teams so nobody stood inside the rope's loop. Nia watched the float from the boat and signaled when the strain was even. On the second pull, the log rose slowly through the green water. Little crabs abandoned it in a shower. The volunteers lowered it onto the sand instead of letting it swing. Beneath it, the grille was bent but clear. Water surged outward for a moment and stopped. The closed gate was still holding the main reservoir. Arun gave the inlet a careful inspection, then raised both hands to show the shore crew that the outlet was ready. Nia felt the first small piece of the puzzle settle into place.

Back beneath the market, the water had reached the bench seat. The coordinator had cleared the square above, and a crew had placed barriers at every entrance to the cellar. Nia fitted the silver token beside the copper one. Arun inserted the final key. All three turned, but the door opened only a hand's breadth. Beyond it lay a chamber containing three narrow wheels connected by a chain. One wheel was frozen by rust. Another spun too freely. The third pulsed with each slow rise of water in the orchard. The bird stood in front of them and spread its damaged wing. Its trailing wire pointed toward the empty place where a regulating spring should have been. Nia remembered the instruction about reservoirs agreeing. These wheels were not locks. They were gauges, and the missing spring had once kept their movements coordinated. Turning the gate by force would break the chain before it opened anything.

Arun searched his tool bag. He had springs for engines, pumps, and bicycle stands, but none with the right tension. Nia searched the notebook. A page had been torn out, leaving only half a diagram. The bird began to tick unevenly. Its warning wheel was running down. For a moment, all of them stood still, listening to the water rise. Then Dev asked why the bird's wing looked exactly like the broken regulator in the drawing. Nia lifted it carefully. Inside the wing, a slender spiral spring shone beneath the brass feathers. Her grandfather had put the spare part inside the warning device. To repair the gate, they would have to dismantle the bird. Nia knew it was machinery, yet she hesitated. It had found her in the dark and led her through the town. Mira touched her shoulder and said that useful things sometimes completed their work by becoming something else.

They carried the bird to the dry ticket counter. Arun arranged the smallest tools on a cloth while Nia drew each step so they could rebuild it later. Dev held the lamp without moving. The tiny screws resisted at first, then loosened with a little oil. Inside the brass chest, they discovered a second folded message. It contained no hidden clue. It simply asked whoever opened the bird to look after the harbor and each other. Nia laughed once, quietly, because after all the maps and mechanisms her grandfather had ended with the instruction he used to give her before every school trip. Arun removed the wing spring. The blue light faded from the bird's eyes. They wrapped its pieces in the towel and carried the spring to the chamber. It fitted the regulator exactly. Once installed, the three wheels began to move at the same patient speed, their marks approaching alignment one fraction at a time.

Above ground, the orchard crew had emptied the shed and uncovered the spillway. Its stone channel was packed with roots. The gardeners argued briefly about which trees might be damaged, then agreed to remove the youngest sapling and save the oldest pear tree. They worked with hand tools because a machine would have cracked the spillway stones. Water seeped around their boots. Mira relayed their progress to the cellar using a line of volunteers on the stairs. Each message was repeated aloud before the next person passed it on. Nobody depended on a single shouted instruction. Nia watched the wheel marks draw together. When all three aligned, a small latch clicked open. She could turn the main handle now, but waited for word from the orchard and inlet. The handle was cold and slippery beneath her palms. For the first time that morning, waiting felt like part of the solution instead of a failure to act.

The inlet crew signaled clear. The orchard crew signaled clear. The coordinator checked that everyone had left the lower channel, then gave permission to begin. Nia and Arun turned the main handle together. It moved a quarter turn and stopped. A deep sound passed through the chamber, like a door opening in another room. Water began to slide beneath their feet toward the hidden passage. They paused, checked the gauges, and turned again. At the orchard, the flood level fell below the shed threshold. At the inlet, brown water poured through the grille and spread into the green sea. The market steps emerged one by one. Nothing dramatic exploded or collapsed. The town simply began to drain. That quiet change felt extraordinary. Dev marked each falling water line on the ticket window until his pencil could barely reach the lowest one. Finally he drew a tiny bird beside the last mark and handed the pencil back to Mira.

They kept watch for two full tide cycles. Volunteers brought soup, dry socks, and folding chairs. The coordinator posted the old survey beside a new list of inspection duties. Arun taught the maintenance crew how to read the three wheels. Mira collected the residents' memories in a ledger, marking uncertain details clearly so stories would not turn into false instructions. Nia took her grandfather's notebook home only long enough to make copies. She gave one to the harbor office and one to the library. The original remained at the lighthouse, where she added drawings of the missing spring and the cleared inlet. She also added the names of everyone who had helped. The bird had guided them to the machinery, but many hands had made the solution possible. By the next morning, fishermen were arguing about weather again, which sounded to Nia like a more reliable sign of recovery than any official announcement.

Repairing the bird took three evenings. Arun made a replacement spring that was stronger than the original, then softened its tension until the wing could fold without straining the brass joints. Dev polished each feather and complained that nobody had included a proper name in the old notebook. Mira suggested calling it Thirteen, but Nia thought that sounded like a warning they no longer needed. They finally chose Wick because it had carried a little light into a confusing morning. When Nia tightened the last screw, Wick blinked once and tipped its head. Its warning wheel no longer connected to the harbor gauge. Instead, Arun had arranged for it to ring a small bell when the lighthouse lamp needed cleaning. There was dignity in ordinary maintenance, Nia thought. A tool should not need a crisis to be useful. Wick hopped onto the windowsill and watched the harbor, its repaired wing catching the warm evening light.

A month later, the town reopened the old waiting room as a small waterworks museum. The iron gate remained visible behind a locked safety screen, with readable instructions beside it. Children traced the underground channel on a floor map. The orchard shed had moved uphill, and a narrow garden followed the newly protected spillway. Nia attended the opening with Wick on her shoulder. At noon, the harbor clock rang twelve clear notes. Everyone paused to listen, then returned to their conversations. Dev asked whether the clock might ever ring thirteen again. Nia told him that it might, but the town would understand the warning next time. On her walk home, she stopped at the inlet and watched fresh water meet the sea. Wick spread both wings in the wind. Beyond the lighthouse, a ferry rounded the wall, following a safe channel toward the busy quay and all the ordinary work waiting there.

That evening, Nia found a fresh page waiting in the shared maintenance ledger. Someone had drawn the town as a collection of listening places: the lighthouse above the water, the workshop beside the ferry, the orchard catching rain, and the market where people exchanged news. Lines joined them like the gears inside Wick. Beneath the drawing, Dev had written a question about who would remember the new instructions when the current volunteers grew old. Nia considered it over supper. The answer could not be another hidden token or a cleverer machine. She wrote back that every school class should visit the gate once, read the gauges, and learn why the inlet must stay clear. Mira added a date for the first visit. Arun volunteered to bring a working model. The coordinator promised a public inspection each autumn, before the storms. By bedtime, the page held contributions from twelve people. Nia left room for many more. Outside, rain began to tap the windows. Wick rang its modest cleaning bell, and she climbed the stairs with a cloth, ready to keep a useful light shining.
